title: Pauri 38, meaning: the true mint
hookLine: let restraint be the furnace, patience the goldsmith, love the crucible; there the Word is minted (Japji 38)
tomorrow: The final salok: air, water, earth

lines: A TRUE COIN, A TRUE MINT.
cards: Pick up any coin and look closely. There's a stamp on it: a face, a date, a design pressed into the metal with enormous force. That stamp is the whole point.
A plain disc is just metal; a struck coin is something people will trust, pass from hand to hand, and spend.

Counterfeiters fake the stamp, so people learned to test coins: ringing them on a counter, weighing them, even biting them. A true coin comes from a true mint. The last line of the last pauri says what's being struck.

teach.h: AWE THE BELLOWS, LOVE THE CRUCIBLE.
teach.b: The workshop so far: restraint the furnace, patience the goldsmith, understanding the anvil, knowledge the tools. The stanza keeps going. Bhau khalaa: awe is the bellows, the deep reverence that keeps the fire breathing.
Agan tap taau: discipline is the fire's heat. Bhaandaa bhaau: love is the crucible, the vessel that holds the molten metal, and into it amrit, the nectar, is poured.
Then the line everything was building toward: gharreeai sabad sachee ttakasaal. In this true mint, the Word is struck.
Sabad, sometimes written shabad, is the Word: the Guru's word, the hymns of the Granth, and for Sikhs something more, because the Guru and the shabad are understood as one.
That's why Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru. So what does it mean to mint the Word? It isn't only read or sung.
It's stamped into a life, by heat and patience and love, until that life is a coin other people can trust. Then the stanza's last lines: jin kau nadar karam tin kaar.
This is the work of those on whom the glance of grace falls.
Nanak nadaree nadar nihaal: the Gracious One, with a glance, fills them with joy. In the stanza's picture, the tools are there to be used, and the stamp comes by grace.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 38 ends with the Word minted in the true mint, and Sikhs honor the shabad as the Guru, present in the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: the Guru's Word, for Sikhs the Guru itself
a holy sound for chanting in silence
any ordinary word, spoken or written

games.q: what's inside Pauri 38 — tap the pairs.

s: in Pauri 38, love is the crucible
bhaandaa bhaau: love is the vessel, and the nectar is poured into it.
Pauri 38 says the Word is minted by effort alone
jin kau nadar karam tin kaar: it's the work of those the glance of grace falls on.
for Sikhs, the Guru and the shabad are understood as one
that's why the Guru Granth Sahib is honored as the living Guru.

games.q: the furnace is hot, the goldsmith patient, the crucible full. what is struck in the true mint of Pauri 38?
games.why: gharreeai sabad sachee ttakasaal: in the true mint, the Word is struck, and it's struck into a life.

practice: Picture one moment when you'll need patience: a slow line, a child's question for the fifth time, a coworker who takes forever. See yourself as the goldsmith there, not rushing the metal, keeping the fire steady.
Breathe like the bellows, a long breath out and a quiet breath in, and let the patience settle into your hands and jaw.

wordCard.voice: Sabad. The Word: the Guru's word, and for Sikhs the Guru itself, struck into a life in the true mint of restraint, patience, awe and love.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 38: the Word is struck in the true mint.
